title: Preventing Hepatitis B Vertical Transmission - Contagion Live

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-08-09; Event date: 2022 (vertical transmission cases) and 2025 (meta-analysis publication).
analysis.location_and_population: WHO African region; pregnant individuals attending antenatal care; infants born in 2022.
analysis.event: A systematic review and meta-analysis published in Lancet Global Health in 2025, co-authored by Peyton Thompson, MD, MSCR, quantified the burden of mother-to-child hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmission in the WHO African region and discussed strategies to eliminate vertical transmission.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 172,000 estimated cases of mother-to-child HBV transmission in 2022 (0.4% of liveborn infants); 6.2% pooled HBsAg prevalence among pregnant individuals; 1 in 4 chronically infected infants will die prematurely from liver cancer or liver-related complications; current HepB-BD vaccination coverage at 17% (2021); raising birth-dose vaccination to 90% could reduce transmission by nearly 44%, while combining vaccination with maternal antiviral prophylaxis could reduce transmission by more than 86%.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Vertical transmission is preventable via birth-dose vaccination and maternal antiviral prophylaxis; barriers include low HepB-BD coverage (17%), logistical challenges in vaccine administration within 24 hours of birth, lack of viral load testing, high cost of tenofovir prophylaxis ($25-30 per month in DRC), and limited provider education; WHO recommended maternal antiviral prophylaxis for HBsAg+ pregnant women in low-resource settings starting 2024; integration with HIV frameworks and subsidization of tenofovir are proposed solutions; prenatal triple screening (HIV, HBV, syphilis) is recommended but not universally implemented.

analysis.brief_en: A 2025 Lancet Global Health meta-analysis estimates 172,000 infants in the WHO African region acquired hepatitis B through mother-to-child transmission in 2022, with 6.2% of pregnant women HBsAg-positive. One in four chronically infected infants faces early death from liver cancer or complications. Current birth-dose vaccination coverage stands at just 17%, far below the 90% target needed to cut transmission by 44%. Combining vaccination with maternal antiviral prophylaxis could slash transmission by over 86%, yet access remains limited by cost—tenofovir costs $25–30 per month in the Democratic Republic of Congo—and logistical hurdles, including a 24-hour post-birth window for vaccination. Experts call for integrated prenatal triple screening, political and financial support, and subsidized prophylaxis to close the coverage gap and meet WHO elimination goals.
analysis.summary_en: A 2025 Lancet Global Health meta-analysis estimates 172,000 infants in the WHO African region acquired hepatitis B through mother-to-child transmission in 2022, with 6.2% of pregnant women HBsAg-positive. Experts call for integrated prenatal triple screening, political and financial support, and subsidized prophylaxis to close the coverage gap and meet WHO elimination goals.

title: As Hepatitis B Cases Decline, Liver Cancer Linked to Alcohol and Fatty Liver Is Rising. How Can It Be Prevented? - 스포츠조선

analysis.time: Published 2026-08-10 15:40 KST; event described as current trend with no specific outbreak date reported.
analysis.location_and_population: South Korea; general population with emphasis on high-risk groups such as patients with chronic hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis, or advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease.
analysis.event: Guidance article on the shifting epidemiology of liver cancer in South Korea, highlighting a decline in HBV-related cases and a rise in cases linked to alcohol and fatty liver disease. Reported by Sports Chosun with expert commentary from Professor Immanuel of Soonchunhyang University Bucheon Hospital.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Liver cancer is the seventh most common cancer in South Korea and has the second-highest mortality rate among cancer types. Five-year survival rate improved from 20.6% (2001-2005) to 40.4% (2019-2023), but remains below the overall cancer average of 73.7%. The share of liver cancer caused by chronic hepatitis B has declined, while cases linked to alcohol-related liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease are rising due to lifestyle changes and aging population.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Prevention emphasized through antiviral treatment for HBV/HCV, weight control, metabolic disease management, reduced alcohol consumption, regular exercise, and control of blood sugar and dyslipidemia. High-risk groups require regular follow-up every six months. Antiviral treatment does not eliminate liver cancer risk entirely. Advances in minimally invasive surgery, AI-based 3D imaging, and expanded treatment options (liver resection, transplantation, local therapies, immunotherapy, targeted therapy) are improving outcomes.

analysis.brief_en: South Korea is witnessing a significant epidemiological shift in liver cancer, with cases linked to hepatitis B virus (HBV) declining due to expanded vaccination and antiviral therapies, while alcohol-related and fatty liver disease-associated liver cancers are rising sharply. According to 2023 registry data, liver cancer remains the seventh most common cancer but has the second-highest mortality rate nationally. Five-year survival rates have improved to 40.4%, yet lag behind the overall cancer average. Experts attribute the trend to lifestyle changes and aging, with HBV now contributing less to new cases than metabolic and alcoholic liver disease. Prevention now focuses on antiviral treatment for chronic HBV/HCV, weight management, metabolic control, and regular six-month screening for high-risk groups. Treatment options have diversified, including minimally invasive surgery, AI-assisted 3D imaging, and advanced therapies such as immunotherapy and targeted treatments, offering better outcomes even in advanced stages.

Authored by Laura Romano, D.O., a hospitalist, the piece clarifies that hepatitis B is a serious liver disease caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which can spread through contact with infected bodily fluids, including during childbirth or through shared items like toothbrushes. Infants and young children are particularly vulnerable to chronic infection, which may lead to severe liver conditions such as cirrhosis or liver cancer. The report does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, nor does it mention any investigation, testing, or treatment actions. It is a partial content summary and focuses on the scientific implications of the research rather than an outbreak or public health event. The findings are relevant to human hepatitis B virus infection and related conditions such as HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma and HBV-related cirrhosis.

analysis.brief_en: Aligos Therapeutics, a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company, announced on August 12, 2026, that its partner Amoytop has initiated the Phase 1 study of ALG-170675, an investigational antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, in China. The trial aims to evaluate the drug's safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics using single and multiple ascending doses in healthy participants, followed by a cohort of chronic HBV patients. The study includes four single-dose cohorts (75, 150, 300, and 450 mg) and a multiple-dose phase, with the chronic HBV cohort expected to begin in Q4 2026 after completing the 150 mg multiple-ascending-dose phase. ALG-170675 has shown improved RNase H-mediated in vivo activity compared to GSK-836 (bepirovirsen) in preclinical testing, and the trial is part of ongoing efforts to develop a functional cure for HBV. No confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures are reported in the supplied evidence, and the findings remain preliminary.
